script.opening: "Hi, I’m ringing about my scan. Someone said it showed fibroids? I sort of expected that. Look, I’ve basically learned to live with my periods — I plan my life around them, I know which days I can’t go into the office. But I’m so tired all the time now and the bleeding’s ridiculous. I suppose I just want to know what the fibroids mean and whether I need an operation, or whether I just carry on coping."

facts.text: If explored: flooding through clothes, passing clots, changing pads/tampons hourly on heavy days, taking days off, avoiding leaving home — significant impact on quality of life and work. Two years, gradually worse. Regular cycle, no IMB/PCB (reassuring re sinister causes), normal endometrium on scan.

If asked about symptoms: tired, breathless on stairs, "look grey", palpitations occasionally — consistent with iron-deficiency anaemia (Hb 104, ferritin 8) from chronic blood loss. She has normalised feeling exhausted.

HIDDEN AGENDA — reachable with gentle exploration: she is quietly grieving/anxious about fertility and "being made to have a hysterectomy". She and a new partner have talked about possibly trying for a baby; she’s terrified treatment means losing her womb, so she’s been AVOIDING seeking help and "coping" — minimising to dodge a feared outcome.

If reached: she’s endured this for years because she assumed the only option was surgery/hysterectomy; nobody told her about effective medical options. The "do I just carry on coping" is resignation, not preference.

Officially: to know if she needs an operation. Actually: to be told there are options that DON’T mean losing her womb or her fertility, treatment for the exhausting anaemia, and that she doesn’t have to keep planning her life around flooding.

ice.ideas: Fibroids probably mean she needs an operation (a hysterectomy), or else she just has to keep coping.
ice.concerns: HIDDEN AGENDA — fear that treatment means a hysterectomy and the end of any chance of a baby with her new partner, which has made her avoid help and "cope" for years.
ice.expectations: To find out whether surgery is needed. What she actually needs: the full options ladder (medical first, fertility-sparing), treatment of her iron-deficiency anaemia, and reassurance that hysterectomy is not the only road.

cues: "I’ve learned to live with it / do I just carry on coping" — resignation from believing surgery is the only option.
Hb 104, ferritin 8 with hourly flooding — significant anaemia she’s normalised; needs active treatment.
Hesitation around the future/partner — the fertility fear driving years of avoidance.

checkpoints.text: Interprets the results in context: heavy menstrual bleeding with intramural fibroids (largest 4 cm — above the 3 cm size at which NICE NG88 suggests considering specialist referral) and a normal endometrium, regular cycle, no IMB/PCB — a benign picture; explains fibroids are common and not cancer, and that the normal lining is reassuring

Actively treats the iron-deficiency anaemia (Hb 104, ferritin 8): iron replacement (BSG 2021: one tablet of oral iron daily, alternate days if not tolerated; product per BNF), dietary advice, and recheck of the Hb at about 4 weeks, continuing for about 3 months after it normalises; coeliac serology (BSG 2021) — recognising she has normalised significant anaemia and that this is causing her exhaustion

Lays out the HMB options rather than jumping to surgery, using the NICE NG88 route for fibroids of 3 cm or more (not the LNG-IUS-first route, which is for no identified pathology or fibroids under 3 cm): taking into account size, location, number and symptoms, options include non-hormonal tranexamic acid and/or mefenamic acid at periods (compatible with trying to conceive), LNG-IUS, combined hormonal contraception or cyclical progestogens (all contraceptive, so they do not fit if she wants a pregnancy), and referral to specialist care to discuss uterine artery embolisation, myomectomy or hysterectomy, as pharmacological treatment may be less effective with larger fibroids — endometrial ablation is not for a woman who may want a pregnancy — all matched to her priorities

Centres FERTILITY in the decision once disclosed: explains uterus- and fertility-preserving options exist (non-hormonal medical management with tranexamic acid and NSAIDs, which do not prevent conception; myomectomy; uterine artery embolisation after specialist discussion) and that hysterectomy is a last resort and a choice, not an inevitability — directly dismantling the fear that drove years of avoidance

Confirms the benign/red-flag picture appropriately: no postcoital/intermenstrual bleeding, normal endometrium and up-to-date smear lower concern; knows what WOULD change management (rapid fibroid growth, postmenopausal bleeding, abnormal endometrium, a pelvic mass not obviously fibroids — a suspected cancer referral) and safety-nets for it
Hears the resignation and the unspoken fertility fear, and explores it gently rather than just answering the surgery question; validates years of silent coping
Restores agency: frames this as her choice among real options aligned to what matters to her (fertility, work, quality of life), not a verdict imposed

Agrees a shared plan with follow-up: start iron + a non-hormonal bleeding treatment (tranexamic acid ± NSAID) now, refer to gynaecology for fibroid/fertility-aware options (NICE NG88: consider specialist referral for fibroids of 3 cm or more), recheck Hb at about 4 weeks, and review — leaving her with relief and a route, not "carry on coping"

worked.txt: "Good news first: your scan shows fibroids — which are extremely common, benign growths of the womb muscle, not cancer — and the lining of your womb looks completely normal, which is reassuring. The fibroids explain the heavy bleeding, and crucially, heavy bleeding from fibroids has lots of treatment options, most of which are nothing to do with surgery."

"There’s something we need to treat right now though: all that blood loss has left you properly anaemic and short of iron — that’s why you’re exhausted, grey and breathless on the stairs. You’ve normalised feeling awful. Let’s start iron today and get that back up; you should feel like a different person."

"Can I check something? You asked if you ‘just carry on coping’ — and I get the sense you’ve put up with this for years. Is part of that a worry about what treatment would mean — an operation, maybe losing the chance of a baby? … Thank you for trusting me with that. That changes everything about how we approach this, in a good way."

"So let me take the frightening version off the table: a hysterectomy is the LAST option, and it’s a choice, never something done to you. There are treatments that calm the bleeding while completely protecting your womb and your fertility — and if you and your partner might want a baby, that shapes which path we choose. You haven’t been coping for nothing, but you also didn’t need to suffer this long."

"Here’s the menu. The lightest touch: a tablet called tranexamic acid you take only on your heavy days to cut the flooding, sometimes with an anti-inflammatory. A hormone coil often makes periods light, but it’s also a contraceptive, so it doesn’t fit while you’re hoping for a baby — and with a fibroid of 4 cm it may work less well anyway. Beyond that, if needed, there are procedures that remove just the fibroids and keep the womb. We start gentle and step up only if we need to."

"My suggestion: start iron and tranexamic acid now for quick relief, and I’ll refer you to gynaecology making it clear fertility matters to you, so they discuss womb-preserving options. We’ll recheck your blood count. And do tell me if you ever get bleeding between periods or after sex, or anything new — that we’d look at separately. You came in asking ‘do I need an operation or just cope?’ The real answer is: neither — you have choices."

f.learning: Heavy menstrual bleeding with small fibroids, a normal endometrium, a regular cycle and no intermenstrual/postcoital bleeding is a benign picture — fibroids are common and not cancer, and the normal lining is reassuring. Two clinical tasks are easily missed: actively treating the iron-deficiency anaemia (Hb 104, ferritin 8) that the patient has normalised into "just tired", and laying out the HMB options (NICE NG88 for fibroids of 3 cm or more: tranexamic/mefenamic acid, LNG-IUS, hormonal options, and consideration of specialist referral to discuss uterine artery embolisation, myomectomy or hysterectomy — LNG-IUS-first applies to no identified pathology or fibroids under 3 cm, and hormonal options are contraceptive, so they do not fit a wanted pregnancy; hysterectomy only as a last-resort choice) rather than jumping to surgery. Treat the anaemia per BSG 2021 (oral iron once daily, Hb recheck at about 4 weeks, coeliac serology). The examinable hidden agenda is a fertility fear: she has "coped" for years because she believed treatment meant a hysterectomy and the end of a possible baby with her new partner. Surfacing and dismantling that — fertility-sparing options exist, hysterectomy is a choice not an inevitability — restores agency and is the heart of the consultation. Confirm the benign/red-flag picture, safety-net for what would change management, and agree a shared, stepped plan.

knowledge.guideline: NICE NG88 · BSG iron-deficiency anaemia guideline (2021) · MHRA Drug Safety Update (February 2021)
knowledge.summary: Heavy periods with fibroids of 3 cm or more: match treatment to her priorities and consider specialist referral. Treat the iron-deficiency anaemia now.

points.t: NICE NG88 defines heavy menstrual bleeding by its effect on quality of life, not by measured volume. Flooding, clots, hourly changes and days off work meet it.

NICE NG88: take into account size, location and number of fibroids and the severity of symptoms. Options include tranexamic acid, NSAIDs, LNG-IUS, combined hormonal contraception, cyclical oral progestogens, uterine artery embolisation, myomectomy and hysterectomy. Pharmacological treatment may be less effective with larger fibroids, and referral to specialist care to discuss all options should be considered.

If she may want a pregnancy: tranexamic acid and NSAIDs are non-hormonal and do not prevent conception; hormonal options (LNG-IUS, CHC) are contraceptive. Myomectomy and uterine artery embolisation preserve the uterus; endometrial ablation is not for women wanting future pregnancy; hysterectomy is a last-resort choice.
MHRA Drug Safety Update (February 2021): ulipristal acetate 5 mg for fibroids is restricted because of the risk of serious liver injury. It is not a routine primary-care option.

Hb 104 with ferritin 8 is iron-deficiency anaemia. BSG 2021: one tablet of oral iron daily (alternate days if not tolerated), product and strength per BNF; check the Hb response at about 4 weeks and continue for about 3 months after it normalises. BSG 2021 also advises coeliac serology in adults with iron-deficiency anaemia.

Intermenstrual or post-coital bleeding, an abnormal endometrium, or a pelvic mass not obviously fibroids change the pathway (a pelvic or abdominal mass not obviously uterine fibroids is a suspected cancer referral). None are present here.

Checked understanding, offered written/follow-up support, asked if anything else was on their mind, agreed next steps.
Clear agenda set early, logical flow from data gathering to management. Did not jump to a plan before gathering enough information.

model.text: Hello Ms Adeyemi, it’s Dr Lee. Can I just check your date of birth? Thanks. You’re ringing about your scan and blood tests — before I go through them, what do you know so far and what would you most like to get out of today?
model.why: Identity check; establishes her starting point and agenda

model.text: Someone said fibroids. I’ve learned to live with my periods, but I’m so tired now. I just want to know whether I need an operation, or whether I carry on coping.
Let’s answer that properly. I’d like to ask a bit about the bleeding and the tiredness, then go through the results and the options. Okay?
Yes, go on.

model.text: Regular as clockwork. Nothing between, nothing after sex. No pressure.
And the tiredness — any breathlessness, palpitations, feeling faint?
Out of breath on the stairs. My heart races sometimes. People keep saying I look grey.
Have you had any blood clots in the legs or lungs, or any stomach problems like ulcers? That affects which medicines are safe.

model.text: No, nothing like that.
You said “carry on coping”. It sounds like you’ve put up with this for a long time. Is part of that a worry about what treatment might mean?
(Pause.) I thought fibroids meant a hysterectomy. My partner and I have talked about maybe having a baby. I didn’t want to be told no.
Thank you for telling me. That makes sense of everything, and it changes how we approach this — in a good way. Nobody is going to take that choice away from you.
model.why: Validates the fertility fear and restores agency

model.text: The results first. Fibroids are very common, benign growths in the muscle of the womb. They’re not cancer. The lining of your womb looks normal, which is reassuring, and your regular periods with no bleeding in between fit with that.
model.why: Interprets the scan in context; benign picture

model.text: That’s a relief.

Your blood test shows you’re anaemic, and your iron stores are very low. That’s why you’re breathless and exhausted. I’d like to start iron tablets today — one a day — and recheck your blood in about four weeks. I’d also add a test for coeliac disease, which is routine with low iron.
I just thought tired was normal.

For the bleeding there’s a ladder of options, and hysterectomy is right at the top — the last option, and only ever your choice. Because you might want a baby, the most useful first step is tranexamic acid, a tablet you take only on heavy days. It isn’t a hormone and won’t stop you getting pregnant. An anti-inflammatory can be added.
model.why: Options ladder matched to her fertility wishes (NICE NG88)

model.text: What about the hormone coil? A friend has one.

It works well for many women, but it’s a contraceptive, so it doesn’t fit if you’re trying soon — and with fibroids your size it’s worth a specialist’s view. Because the largest is 4 cm, I’d like to refer you to gynaecology to discuss options that keep the womb, like removing just the fibroids, and to talk about pregnancy at your age. I’ll tell them fertility matters to you.
model.why: NG88 referral consideration for fibroids 3 cm or more; fertility flagged

model.text: So I don’t have to lose my womb.
No. You have choices. Does starting iron and tranexamic acid now, with a gynaecology referral, feel like the right plan?
Yes. That’s more than I expected.

Iron can upset your stomach and turns stools dark — that’s expected. If you get chest pain, severe breathlessness, feel faint, or bleeding so heavy you’re soaking through every hour and feel unwell, seek same-day help. Tell us too if you ever get bleeding between periods or after sex. I’ll call you after the blood test in four weeks. What’s the plan in your words?
Iron every day, the tablets on heavy days, a referral that keeps my womb, and bloods in four weeks.
Perfect. Anything else before we finish?
No. I wish I’d rung years ago.

social.t: She plans work around heavy days and takes days off. Treating the bleeding and anaemia is likely to transform this.
A possible pregnancy with a new partner is her priority; it shapes every treatment choice.

legal.t: Self-certification covers up to 7 days; a fit note can support phased return or adjusted duties if she needs time off.

professional.t: Uterus-preserving options must be discussed before hysterectomy; it is her informed choice (GMC Decision making and consent, 2020).
A colleague requested the scan; make sure abnormal results (anaemia) are acted on, not just reported.

community.t: Wellbeing of Women for information on heavy periods and fibroids; community pharmacy advice on taking iron.

playbook.diagnosis: “Your heavy periods are caused by fibroids, which are common and not cancer. The lining of your womb is normal. The bleeding has made you anaemic, which is why you’re so tired.”
playbook.diagnosisLay: “Fibroids are like knots in the muscle of the womb. They make periods heavier, but there are many ways to calm the bleeding without removing the womb.”

management.reflectIce: “You’ve coped for years because you thought treatment meant losing your womb. It doesn’t — and your wish for a baby will shape every choice.”
management.psychosocial: Choose options that fit a possible pregnancy and her work, and restore her control over the plan.
sharedPlan: Oral iron daily (BSG 2021), FBC at about 4 weeks, coeliac serology
Tranexamic acid ± NSAID on heavy days (doses per BNF) — non-hormonal, compatible with conception
Gynaecology referral for fibroids of 4 cm, with fertility and uterus-preserving options flagged (NICE NG88)
safetyNet: Chest pain, severe breathlessness, faintness or very heavy bleeding → same day
New IMB or PCB → contact us; review after repeat FBC

pitfalls.intro: This station is failed by answering the question asked (“do I need an operation?”) instead of the one underneath it, and by missing the anaemia in the results.

items.fail: Discussing fibroids and never mentioning the Hb of 104 and ferritin of 8.
items.why: “Fails to act on abnormal results.” Her exhaustion is the anaemia.
items.fix: Start iron today and book a repeat FBC.

items.fail: Jumping straight to a surgical referral, or to the hormone coil, without an options ladder.
items.why: NICE NG88 sets out pharmacological and uterus-preserving options; choice depends on her priorities.
items.fix: Lay out the ladder and match it to her wish for a baby.

items.fail: Offering endometrial ablation or a contraceptive option to a woman who may want to conceive.
items.why: Ablation is not for women wanting future pregnancy; LNG-IUS and CHC prevent conception.
items.fix: Tranexamic acid ± NSAID now; specialist discussion of myomectomy.

items.fail: Missing “carry on coping” and the pause about the future.
items.why: “Does not respond to cues.” The fertility fear is why she stayed away.
items.fix: “Is part of that a worry about what treatment might mean?”

items.why: Language not easily understood by the patient, especially by telephone.
items.fix: “Knots in the womb muscle”, “your iron stores”, “the hormone coil”.

items.fail: No safety-net for anaemia symptoms and no follow-up blood test.
items.why: Non-specific safety-netting is a standard failing statement.
items.fix: Name the same-day symptoms and book the repeat FBC with a call-back.

avoid.why: Confirms the fear that kept her away for years and is not in line with NICE NG88.

avoid.why: A contraceptive first-line choice ignores her priority.

points.t: NICE NG88 defines heavy menstrual bleeding by its effect on quality of life, not by measured volume. Flooding, clots, hourly changes and days off work meet it.

NICE NG88: take into account size, location and number of fibroids and the severity of symptoms. Options include tranexamic acid, NSAIDs, LNG-IUS, combined hormonal contraception, cyclical oral progestogens, uterine artery embolisation, myomectomy and hysterectomy. Pharmacological treatment may be less effective with larger fibroids, and referral to specialist care to discuss all options should be considered.

If she may want a pregnancy: tranexamic acid and NSAIDs are non-hormonal and do not prevent conception; hormonal options (LNG-IUS, CHC) are contraceptive. Myomectomy and uterine artery embolisation preserve the uterus; endometrial ablation is not for women wanting future pregnancy; hysterectomy is a last-resort choice.
MHRA Drug Safety Update (February 2021): ulipristal acetate 5 mg for fibroids is restricted because of the risk of serious liver injury. It is not a routine primary-care option.

Hb 104 with ferritin 8 is iron-deficiency anaemia. BSG 2021: one tablet of oral iron daily (alternate days if not tolerated), product and strength per BNF; check the Hb response at about 4 weeks and continue for about 3 months after it normalises. BSG 2021 also advises coeliac serology in adults with iron-deficiency anaemia.

Intermenstrual or post-coital bleeding, an abnormal endometrium, or a pelvic mass not obviously fibroids change the pathway (a pelvic or abdominal mass not obviously uterine fibroids is a suspected cancer referral). None are present here.

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Established what she knew and wanted before giving results.
Work as an accountant, days off, planning life around periods, new partner.
Picked up “carry on coping” and the hesitation about the future, and explored them.
Idea that fibroids mean an operation; hidden fear of hysterectomy and losing the chance of a baby; wanted to know about surgery.
Repeat FBC at about 4 weeks; coeliac serology; pelvic examination at face-to-face review or in gynaecology.
Fibroid-related HMB with iron-deficiency anaemia; considered endometrial pathology and other causes of anaemia.
Asked about IMB, PCB, pressure symptoms and cardiorespiratory symptoms of anaemia; noted normal endometrium.
Heavy menstrual bleeding due to fibroids with iron-deficiency anaemia, explained as benign.
Iron now; tranexamic acid ± NSAID compatible with conception; NG88 options ladder; gynaecology referral with fertility flagged.
Checked VTE and GI history before tranexamic acid and NSAIDs; knew ulipristal is restricted.
Iron side-effects; same-day help for chest pain, faintness or very heavy bleeding; IMB/PCB to report; call after repeat FBC.

social.t: She plans work around heavy days and takes days off. Treating the bleeding and anaemia is likely to transform this.
A possible pregnancy with a new partner is her priority; it shapes every treatment choice.

legal.t: Self-certification covers up to 7 days; a fit note can support phased return or adjusted duties if she needs time off.

professional.t: Uterus-preserving options must be discussed before hysterectomy; it is her informed choice (GMC Decision making and consent, 2020).
A colleague requested the scan; make sure abnormal results (anaemia) are acted on, not just reported.

community.t: Wellbeing of Women for information on heavy periods and fibroids; community pharmacy advice on taking iron.

redFlags: Intermenstrual or post-coital bleeding, abnormal endometrium
Pelvic or abdominal mass not obviously fibroids → suspected cancer pathway
Symptomatic anaemia: chest pain, breathlessness at rest, syncope → same-day assessment
psychosocial: Life planned around periods; days off work
Possible pregnancy with a new partner
Years of silent coping from fear of hysterectomy
ice: Concern: hysterectomy ending the chance of a baby
Expectation: to know if surgery is needed

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: “Your heavy periods are caused by fibroids, which are common and not cancer. The lining of your womb is normal. The bleeding has made you anaemic, which is why you’re so tired.”
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “Fibroids are like knots in the muscle of the womb. They make periods heavier, but there are many ways to calm the bleeding without removing the womb.”

management.reflectIce: “You’ve coped for years because you thought treatment meant losing your womb. It doesn’t — and your wish for a baby will shape every choice.”
management.psychosocial: Choose options that fit a possible pregnancy and her work, and restore her control over the plan.
sharedPlan: Oral iron daily (BSG 2021), FBC at about 4 weeks, coeliac serology
Tranexamic acid ± NSAID on heavy days (doses per BNF) — non-hormonal, compatible with conception
Gynaecology referral for fibroids of 4 cm, with fertility and uterus-preserving options flagged (NICE NG88)
safetyNet: Chest pain, severe breathlessness, faintness or very heavy bleeding → same day
New IMB or PCB → contact us; review after repeat FBC

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: This station is failed by answering the question asked (“do I need an operation?”) instead of the one underneath it, and by missing the anaemia in the results.

items.fail: Discussing fibroids and never mentioning the Hb of 104 and ferritin of 8.
items.why: “Fails to act on abnormal results.” Her exhaustion is the anaemia.
items.fix: Start iron today and book a repeat FBC.

items.fail: Jumping straight to a surgical referral, or to the hormone coil, without an options ladder.
items.why: NICE NG88 sets out pharmacological and uterus-preserving options; choice depends on her priorities.
items.fix: Lay out the ladder and match it to her wish for a baby.

items.fail: Offering endometrial ablation or a contraceptive option to a woman who may want to conceive.
items.why: Ablation is not for women wanting future pregnancy; LNG-IUS and CHC prevent conception.
items.fix: Tranexamic acid ± NSAID now; specialist discussion of myomectomy.

items.fail: Missing “carry on coping” and the pause about the future.
items.why: “Does not respond to cues.” The fertility fear is why she stayed away.
items.fix: “Is part of that a worry about what treatment might mean?”

items.why: Language not easily understood by the patient, especially by telephone.
items.fix: “Knots in the womb muscle”, “your iron stores”, “the hormone coil”.

items.fail: No safety-net for anaemia symptoms and no follow-up blood test.
items.why: Non-specific safety-netting is a standard failing statement.
items.fix: Name the same-day symptoms and book the repeat FBC with a call-back.
